title: Wi-Fi Password Best Practices: Securing Your Home and Office Network
excerpt: A weak Wi-Fi password doesn't just let neighbors steal your bandwidth — it puts every device on your network at risk. Here's how to properly secure your router and wireless network.
content:
Why Your Wi-Fi Password Matters More Than You Think

When someone gets onto your Wi-Fi network, they're inside your network perimeter. They can potentially see unencrypted traffic, attempt to access network-attached storage, printers, and smart home devices, and use your IP address for illegal activity. A weak router admin password means they could change your DNS settings to intercept all your web traffic, including banking sites.

The good news: securing your Wi-Fi properly takes about 20 minutes and the protection lasts years.

Setting a Strong Wi-Fi Password

Your Wi-Fi password (technically the WPA Pre-Shared Key) should be at least 20 characters. Use a mix of uppercase, lowercase, numbers, and symbols. You can use our password generator to create one — then write it down on a piece of paper taped inside a kitchen cabinet. You'll only need to type it when connecting new devices, and a physical note is much safer than a simple password.

Avoid these common mistakes:

  • Using your address, family name, or phone number as the password
  • Using the default password printed on the router (these are often predictable or appear in public databases)
  • Using 'password123' or any simple variation
  • Using the same password as your router admin interface

Choosing the Right Security Protocol

Your router's security protocol matters as much as the password. In your router admin interface (usually accessible at 192.168.1.1 or 192.168.0.1), look for Wireless Security settings and choose:

  • WPA3 — The current standard. If your router and devices support it, use this. WPA3 is significantly harder to crack than older protocols.
  • WPA2/WPA3 Mixed Mode — Good if you have older devices that don't support WPA3. Newer devices use WPA3, older ones fall back to WPA2.
  • WPA2 (AES/CCMP) — Acceptable if WPA3 isn't available. Make sure you're using AES, not TKIP.
  • WEP or WPA (TKIP) — These are obsolete and easily cracked in minutes. If your router only supports these, it's time to replace it.

Changing the Router Admin Password

This is critical and frequently overlooked. Your router has a separate admin password used to access its settings interface. The default is often printed on the router ('admin/admin', 'admin/password', or similar) and is publicly documented for every router model.

Log into your router (check the sticker on the bottom for the admin URL and default credentials) and change the admin password immediately. Make it different from your Wi-Fi password and store it in your password manager.

Setting Up a Guest Network

Create a separate guest network for visitors, smart home devices (TVs, speakers, cameras), and IoT devices. Here's why this matters:

  • Guests get internet access without seeing your main network devices
  • Smart home devices, which often have poor security, are isolated from your computers and phones
  • If a smart device gets compromised, the damage is contained to the guest network

Set a separate, moderately strong password for the guest network (you'll share this more often, so you need to remember it or have it easily accessible).

Other Router Security Steps

  • Update your router's firmware. Manufacturers release security patches, but routers don't auto-update by default. Check your router's admin interface for a firmware update option, or look up your model on the manufacturer's site.
  • Disable WPS. Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS) is a feature with known vulnerabilities. Turn it off in your router's wireless settings.
  • Disable remote management. Unless you specifically need to access your router from outside your home, disable this feature. It reduces your attack surface.
  • Check connected devices periodically. Most routers show a list of connected devices in the admin interface. Review this occasionally to spot anything unexpected.

What to Do If Your Network May Be Compromised

If you suspect someone has unauthorized access to your network: change both your Wi-Fi password and your router admin password immediately. Review the list of connected devices and kick any you don't recognize. Check your router's DNS settings — they should point to your ISP's DNS servers or a known public DNS like 1.1.1.1 (Cloudflare) or 8.8.8.8 (Google), not an unknown IP.

Recommended Tools

Store your router admin credentials in a password manager so you never have to write them in an obvious place. NordPass is an excellent option with a strong free tier. For additional network protection — especially on public Wi-Fi when traveling — a VPN is essential. See all our picks on the recommended tools page.
